evidence.label: The ℓ¹-Bass Conjecture for Discrete Groups
The Bass trace conjecture and the characteristic-zero Kaplansky idempotent conjecture

headline: Idempotents in group rings carry no trace at infinite-order elements, for every group; Kaplansky's problem follows.
scope: Complex group rings of every discrete group; idempotents over characteristic-zero domains for torsion-free groups; and the ℓ¹ group algebra.
plain: An idempotent is an element e with e times e equal to e. Bass conjectured that idempotent matrices over a group ring leave no trace on elements of infinite order. This family proves it for complex group rings of every group. It deduces that torsion-free groups have only the idempotents 0 and 1 over characteristic-zero coefficients. A second paper claims the same for the larger ℓ¹ algebra.
doesNot: This does not settle Kaplansky's idempotent problem for coefficients of positive characteristic, such as the integers mod 2.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.significanceWhy: It removes every hypothesis on the group from two conjectures that were open for decades and checked case by case.

explanation:
Take a group with two elements: 1 and a flip s, where flipping twice gives 1. Form sums like a + b·s with complex numbers a and b, and multiply them out using s·s = 1. This is the group ring. Now try e = ½ + ½s. Squaring gives ¼ + ½s + ¼s·s, which is ¼ + ½s + ¼, or ½ + ½s again. So e·e = e. An element with this property is called an idempotent.

The trick used that s has finite order: some power of s is 1. Try the same with a group where nothing but 1 has finite order, such as the whole numbers under addition, written as powers of t. Then (½ + ½t)² is ¼ + ½t + ¼t², which is not ½ + ½t. Kaplansky's idempotent problem asks whether this is always so. In a group with no elements of finite order other than 1, are 0 and 1 the only idempotents? Such a group is called torsion-free.

Bass asked a sharper question. Take an idempotent square matrix over the group ring. Add up its diagonal entries and sort the coefficients by conjugacy class. A conjugacy class is the set of elements that become each other after a change of viewpoint, g turned into h·g·h⁻¹. This sorted sum is the Hattori–Stallings trace. The Bass trace conjecture says its coefficients are zero on every class of infinite order[1]. Finite-order classes may be nonzero. In the flip example, e has coefficient ½ on the class of s[2].

Many cases were known. Bass proved the vanishing for linear groups, groups made of invertible matrices[3]. Farrell and Linnell proved the complex statement for elementary amenable groups[4]. Berrick, Chatterji and Mislin covered amenable groups through a stronger statement on a larger algebra[5]. For idempotents, Formanek handled torsion-free groups with a chain condition on subgroups[6]. Each method needed a hypothesis on the group.

One paper proves the complex Bass trace conjecture for every group, with no hypothesis[7]. For torsion-free groups it deduces Kaplansky's conjecture in characteristic zero[8]. That means coefficients like whole numbers, rationals or complex numbers, and any domain built on them. A second paper claims the ℓ¹ version[9]. There the sums may have infinitely many terms, as long as the sizes of their coefficients add up to a finite number. It claims the trace lives on finitely many finite-order classes[10].

The single obstacle is that the group is arbitrary. Earlier methods asked the group to be amenable, hyperbolic or of finite dimension in some sense. The group-ring paper turns one trace coefficient into a number computed on a high-dimensional geometric object[11]. It then shows that number must be zero in high enough dimension, by cutting the object into small pieces[12]. For the ℓ¹ paper, products of coefficients can involve elements far from the identity[13]. Its estimates have to stay under control as the number of factors grows.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has a formal proof of the complex Bass trace conjecture for every group. It also covers the torsion-free trace identity and Kaplansky's conjecture over every characteristic-zero domain. The ℓ¹ result lies outside that check, so for it the paper only claims a proof. No specialist review of either paper has been published.
hypeCheck: The group-ring Bass conjecture and Kaplansky's characteristic-zero case have Lean proofs. The ℓ¹ version is only claimed. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: Formal sums of group elements with numerical coefficients, multiplied using the group's own rule.
An element e with e times e equal to e. 0 and 1 always qualify.
A group where no element other than the identity returns to the identity when repeated.
All elements of the form h·g·h⁻¹ for a fixed g, as h ranges over the group.
The sum of an idempotent matrix's diagonal entries, with coefficients grouped by conjugacy class.
Coefficients in which adding 1 to itself never gives 0, like the integers or the complex numbers.
Infinite sums over the group whose coefficient sizes add up to a finite number.

claims.sourceQuote: The complex group-ring Bass conjecture asks whether these coefficients vanish on every infinite-order conjugacy class, for every group and every class in $K_0(\C G)$; see \cite[Conjecture 2.1]{BCM2004} and \cite[Conjecture 2]{CM2011}.

claims.text: For a finite group the averaging idempotent has coefficient |C|/|F| at every class.
claims.sourceLine: $|C|/|F|$ at every conjugacy class $C$. The conclusion therefore differs
claims.sourceQuote: Finite-order coefficients need not vanish away from the identity: for a finite group $F$, the idempotent $|F|^{-1}\sum_{h\in F}h$ has coefficient $|C|/|F|$ at every conjugacy class $C$. The conclusion therefore differs from the identity-only support assertion for integral group rings.
